blocks.text: Farmed salmon’s changing nutrition

blocks.caption: Of salmon eaten worldwide is farmed
blocks.text: Nearly 70%

items: THE FINDING — A new USDA-led study found that farmed salmon contained considerably less omega-3 fatty acid than older nutritional figures suggest.
THE LIMIT — The sample was too small to justify changing dietary guidance; the researchers call for a broader, representative study.
THE MECHANISM — Feed has shifted from small marine fish toward crops and oils such as soy and canola.
THE TRADE-OFF — That may reduce pressure on forage fish while increasing land-use and emissions impacts.

blocks.text: Farmed salmon production tripled between 2000 and 2020, as health advice and marketing helped make it a global staple. But the feed used to produce more fish has changed as oceans have yielded fewer small species. The result is a possible nutritional decline, alongside new environmental costs on land.

blocks.caption: The share of Norwegian salmon feed ingredients from marine sources
blocks.text: 90% marine-based in 1990; about 23% by 2020

blocks.caption: How the feed shift changes the trade-off
blocks.imagePrompt: A simple flow diagram showing small marine fish and crop ingredients feeding farmed salmon, with two arrows labeled omega-3 and land impact.

blocks.caption: Laura Lee Cascada, Aquaculture Accountability Project
blocks.text: “It’s trading one problem—marine exploitation—for another—land exploitation.”

The study does not show that salmon has stopped being nutritious, nor that official advice should immediately change. It shows that the numbers behind familiar advice may no longer describe today’s farmed fish—and that producing more protein can shift, rather than remove, environmental pressure.

blocks.text: Farmed salmon’s omega-3 edge may be shrinking

blocks.caption: Of salmon eaten is farmed
blocks.text: Nearly 70%

items: THE FINDING — A new USDA-led study found that omega-3 levels in farmed salmon have fallen considerably.
THE LIMIT — The sample was too small to justify changing dietary guidance; researchers call for a broader study.
THE MECHANISM — Feed has shifted from small marine fish toward soy, canola and other land-grown ingredients.
THE TRADE-OFF — Pressure on small fish has eased, but crop-based feed brings land-use and emissions concerns.

blocks.text: Farmed salmon production tripled from 2000 to 2020. As demand rose, feed makers increasingly replaced marine ingredients with crops and oils. That may help reduce pressure on forage fish, but it also changes the nutritional profile consumers were encouraged to seek—and can shift environmental costs onto farmland and forests.
In Norway, marine-based feed ingredients fell from 90% in 1990 to about 23% in 2020.

The study does not show that farmed salmon has stopped being nutritious, or that existing advice should immediately change. It shows that older omega-3 assumptions may no longer describe today’s fish, while the industry’s environmental trade-offs remain unresolved.
Read the full report and the debate over offshore salmon farming.

blocks.text: BepiColombo Nears Mercury

blocks.caption: Time since launch in 2018
blocks.text: 8 years

items: THE MILESTONE — BepiColombo has entered the final stretch of its journey to Mercury.
THE ROUTE — It used plasma propulsion and flybys of Earth, Venus and Mercury to change its velocity and trajectory.
THE NEXT STEP — On its next encounter later this year, the spacecraft is expected to be moving slowly enough for Mercury's gravity to capture it into orbit.
THE CATCH — Reaching Mercury and entering orbit requires more energy, or delta-v, than sending a spacecraft on a flyby to Pluto.

blocks.caption: A route shaped by gravity and propulsion

blocks.text: The long route is the point: Mercury is close to the Sun, but its speed and gravity make orbital arrival unusually demanding. BepiColombo's final approach is the payoff from years of carefully timed manoeuvres, not a straight trip inward.

blocks.text: Competitive Pokémon needs a Switch

blocks.caption: Champions downloads across platforms
blocks.text: 25 million

items: THE GAP — Champions plays nearly identically on phones and Switch, but regional tournaments and above still require Switch hardware.
THE REASON — Pokémon producer Masaaki Hoshino cited Switch 2’s sharper graphics and the complexity of supporting many mobile devices.
THE WORKAROUND — Streamed matches can use tournament-provided hardware and replicated teams, according to the rules handbook.
THE STAKES — Players can build tournament-ready teams on mobile, but may reach Worlds without owning the device required to compete.

blocks.text: Mobile already gets players to the starting line. The odd part is that it may not get them to the biggest stage.

The game’s battle calculations run server-side, so cross-platform play works. Mobile is also used in high-level Pokémon Unite competition, suggesting the obstacle is tournament presentation and logistics rather than a fundamental technical barrier.

For a game that presents itself as inclusive and accessible, requiring a Switch at the top level creates a costly final hurdle. That matters more as competitive Pokémon grows beyond its former hotel-ballroom scale.

blocks.text: Competitive Pokémon Needs No Switch

blocks.caption: Champions downloads across platforms
blocks.text: 25 million

items: THE RULE — Mobile works for local tournaments, but regional events and Worlds still require Switch hardware.
THE GAP — The game is otherwise nearly identical and cross-platform.
blocks.text: THE RULE — Mobile works for local tournaments, but regional events and Worlds still require Switch hardware. THE GAP — The game is otherwise nearly identical and cross-platform.

The explanation is mostly about presentation and logistics: Switch 2 looks sharper, while supporting many different phones could complicate events. But that leaves mobile players able to build a championship-ready team without being able to use it on the biggest stage.
Mobile players can qualify for Worlds — then lack the hardware to compete there.

A simple compromise already exists: tournament organisers can provide hardware for streamed matches using a player’s team ID. Other competitive Pokémon games, including Pokémon Unite and Pokémon Go, also show that mobile competition is possible.
The game’s promise is accessibility. Requiring a Switch at the top level undercuts that promise, especially as the console becomes more expensive and millions of players may have started on phones.

blocks.text: Fairphone 6 Plus makes repairability mainstream

items: THE IDEA — Fairphone’s latest phone feels like a normal midrange Android device, while keeping its repairable, ethically minded design.
WHY NOW — Prices have climbed, making a five-year warranty and up to six OS upgrades easier to value.
THE CATCH — IP55 protection, no wireless charging, average speakers and merely adequate battery life remain tradeoffs.

blocks.text: The important shift is that Fairphone’s sustainability pitch no longer requires accepting a dramatically worse phone. The 6 Plus runs smoothly for everyday tasks, uses a near-stock version of Android and avoids bloatware and gimmicky AI features.
You are the AppleCare.

Twelve user-replaceable parts include the battery, screen, USB-C port and all three cameras. Fairphone charges $39.99 for a replacement battery and $89.99 for a display, while comparable repairs elsewhere can cost substantially more.

The phone’s Snapdragon 7S Gen 4 chip handles ordinary use well, though demanding games, some navigation and heavier camera bursts reveal its limits. The cameras are dependable rather than exceptional, and battery life is only average—but replacing the battery is designed to be simple.

A modular back panel can add a wallet or grip, while Fairphone’s Moments switch offers minimalist focus modes. These touches are less seamless than magnetic accessories, but they make the phone feel deliberately useful rather than overstuffed.

The Fairphone 6 Plus is no longer just an ethical compromise. It is a broadly capable phone whose repairability, long support period and lower repair costs give its relatively high price a practical case.

blocks.text: Fairphone 6 Plus reaches the mainstream
THE IDEA — Fairphone’s latest phone feels like a normal midrange Android device, but keeps the company’s repairable design and ethical-materials focus.
REPAIRS — Twelve parts are user-replaceable, including the battery, display, USB-C port, and cameras. A replacement battery costs $39.99; a display costs $89.99.
SUPPORT — The phone includes a five-year warranty and up to six OS upgrades. It supports T-Mobile and AT&T in the US, and worked for the reviewer on Verizon despite lacking certification.
THE CATCH — Battery life is merely adequate, the IP55 rating is below many rivals, and there is no wireless charging. The cameras and performance are competent rather than exceptional.
A phone that is simply fine is the point: its repairability no longer demands the major compromises Fairphone once required.
The Fairphone 6 Plus is a strong choice if long-term repair costs and software support matter more to you than peak cameras, gaming power, or water resistance.

blocks.text: Explore the globe in field recordings

blocks.caption: Earth Garden uses recordings from Freesound.
blocks.text: Around the world through environmental sound

items: THE IDEA — Earth Garden works like Radio Garden, but with environmental audio instead of live radio. Rotate the globe and listen as the reticle reaches new places.
THE SOUND — Hear waves near remote Atlantic islands, crickets in Tanzania and rain on Manhattan streets.
THE CATCH — Freesound makes the collection broad, but clip quality and volume vary. Recordings are also concentrated in the US and Europe, especially the UK.

items: THE IDEA — Earth Garden lets you explore a globe through field recordings from Freesound.
THE SOUNDS — Hear waves, crickets, rain and other environmental audio from locations around the world.
HOW IT WORKS — Rotate the globe or let it spin automatically; a reticle switches recordings as it reaches new points.
THE CATCH — Recording quality and volume vary, and the collection is concentrated in the US and Europe, especially the UK.

blocks.imagePrompt: A clean world globe with a glowing reticle moving between three labeled sound points: Atlantic waves, Tanzania crickets, Manhattan rain.
blocks.text: A globe you listen to, not just look at.
Earth Garden is a small, soothing way to turn geographic browsing into active listening. It also offers optional generic ambient drones, though the underlying recordings can be uneven.
